subject: Modern Monetary Theory and Federal Spending
overview: Host Anna Callahan spoke with economics professor Fadhel Kaboub about Modern Monetary Theory, federal debt, and how currency issuance impacts the financing of large-scale social programs. Kaboub argued that federal spending is constrained by inflation and productive capacity rather than tax revenue or borrowing.

items.title: Introduction to National Debt and MMT
items.summary: Anna Callahan introduced the broadcast and posed foundational questions regarding national debt, borrowing, and potential alternative economic models for funding major public programs.

items.title: Federal Currency Issuance Versus Household Budgeting
items.summary: Fadhel Kaboub explained the core principles of Modern Monetary Theory, contrasting currency-issuing federal governments with currency-using households and municipalities using examples from World War II and the CARES Act.

items.title: Commercial Bank Money Creation and Banking Charters
items.summary: Kaboub described how private banks create money through licensed lending and argued that banking charters should serve a public purpose or be extended to public institutions such as postal banks.

items.title: Inflation Constraints and Funding Public Programs
items.summary: Kaboub outlined how federal spending limits are dictated by available productive capacity and corporate market power rather than tax revenue, arguing that initiatives like Medicare for All, the Green New Deal, and student debt cancellation lower broader economic costs.

items.title: Audience Question on Post-2008 Inflation Rates
items.summary: Kaboub answered an audience question regarding why quantitative easing following 2008 did not produce widespread inflation, attributing the outcome to productive capacity limits, concentrated capital distribution, and consumer debt burdens.

items.title: Closing Remarks and Resources
items.summary: Kaboub and Callahan concluded the program by sharing recommended reading, organizations, and media resources covering Modern Monetary Theory.
